subject: Pathology
vignette: A 29-year-old man is placed in a long leg cast after a tibial fracture and is non-weight-bearing for 10 weeks. On cast removal, the calf of the immobilized leg is visibly smaller than the contralateral calf, and thigh circumference is also reduced. Strength gradually returns with physical therapy, and the limb regains most of its bulk over the next several months.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of muscle loss in the immobilized limb?

options.text: Reduced cell size through increased ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and autophagy
Increased cell number from compensatory stem cell proliferation
Replacement of skeletal muscle by stratified squamous epithelium
An increase in structural proteins and organelles within each myocyte
Necrosis of myocytes with surrounding acute inflammation

explanation_correct: Disuse is a classic cause of atrophy, which is a decrease in tissue mass caused by decreased cell size and/or decreased cell number. Atrophy of muscle works through increased cytoskeleton degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, through autophagy (programmed digestion of damaged or misfolded intracellular proteins), and through reduced protein synthesis. Because the change is a regressive adaptation rather than cell death, function and bulk can be restored once the disuse stimulus is removed, as happened with physical therapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hyperplasia, an increased number of cells from proliferation of stem cells, increases tissue mass; it cannot explain shrinkage of an immobilized limb.
explanation_incorrect.B: Metaplasia replaces one mature cell type with another after stem cell reprogramming, typically in epithelia responding to an irritant; skeletal muscle does not convert to squamous epithelium with disuse.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increased structural proteins and organelles enlarge cells and produce hypertrophy, the opposite of the decrease in size described here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Necrosis involves membrane damage, enzyme leakage, and a local inflammatory reaction; it is a form of cell death, not the reversible, controlled regressive change of disuse atrophy.

educationalObjective: Atrophy is a decrease in tissue mass from reduced cell size (increased ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and autophagy, decreased protein synthesis) and/or cell number, and disuse is a classic cause.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 57-year-old woman undergoes endoscopy for 8 years of weekly heartburn that has been poorly controlled. The distal esophagus shows a salmon-colored mucosal patch above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy reveals columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing the normal stratified squamous epithelium, without atypia.
question: Which of the following best describes this finding?

options.text: Hypertrophy of squamous epithelial cells due to chronic acid exposure
Metaplasia from reprogramming of stem cells, predisposing to adenocarcinoma
Dysplasia with loss of nuclear uniformity and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
Atrophy of the squamous epithelium with thinning of the mucosal layer
Hyperplasia of squamous epithelium with an increased number of basal cells

explanation_correct: Barrett esophagus is the classic example of metaplasia: chronic exposure to gastric acid causes reprogramming of esophageal stem cells so that the normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which tolerates the new stressor better. Metaplasia is an adaptive change, but with persistent insult it may progress to dysplasia and then to esophageal adenocarcinoma, which is why patients with Barrett esophagus undergo surveillance. The absence of atypia on this biopsy means dysplasia is not yet present.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hypertrophy enlarges individual cells and does not change the epithelial cell type; it would thicken the squamous layer rather than replace it with columnar cells.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dysplasia is disordered, precancerous growth with pleomorphism and loss of orientation; the biopsy specifically shows no atypia, so the lesion is metaplasia only.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atrophy thins existing epithelium by shrinking and reducing its cells, but the squamous epithelium has been replaced by a different cell type, which is metaplasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Squamous hyperplasia increases the number of the resident squamous cells but preserves the squamous phenotype; the appearance of goblet cells indicates a change in cell type.

educationalObjective: Barrett esophagus, replacement of distal esophageal squamous epithelium by intestinal columnar epithelium, is the canonical example of metaplasia and can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 63-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history undergoes bronchoscopy for a chronic cough. A brushing of the bronchial mucosa shows that the normal ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium has been replaced by stratified squamous epithelium. There are no atypia, no invasion, and no mass lesion.
question: Which of the following best describes this epithelial change?

options.text: Metaplasia with loss of mucociliary clearance due to tobacco smoke
Dysplasia with disordered growth and pleomorphism
Hyperplasia with an increased number of ciliated columnar cells
Atrophy with reduced thickness of the bronchial epithelium
Neoplastic transformation with invasion of the basement membrane

explanation_correct: Tobacco smoke is the classic irritant that causes reprogramming of respiratory stem cells so that ciliated columnar epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium, a form of metaplasia in the airway. The squamous epithelium survives the smoke better, but it lacks cilia, so mucociliary clearance is impaired and secretions and particulates accumulate. Metaplasia is reversible if the irritant is removed, yet persistent exposure can lead to dysplasia and eventually squamous cell carcinoma; this biopsy shows no atypia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dysplasia is disordered, precancerous growth with pleomorphism, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and loss of orientation; the specimen shows an orderly new cell type without atypia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hyperplasia increases the number of the existing cell type without changing it; here the ciliated columnar cells have been replaced rather than multiplied.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atrophy decreases tissue mass through smaller and fewer cells but leaves the original cell type in place; the finding is a new epithelial phenotype, not thinning of the old one.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neoplastic transformation requires invasive growth through the basement membrane; the change here is confined to the epithelium and is an adaptive response, not a carcinoma.

educationalObjective: Tobacco smoke causes metaplasia of respiratory ciliated columnar epithelium to stratified squamous epithelium, which impairs mucociliary clearance and can progress to dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 41-year-old man sustains a direct blow to the thigh during a soccer match. Six weeks later he presents with a firm, deep, painful mass in the quadriceps. Radiographs show a well-defined area of mature bone formation within the muscle at the site of the hematoma. He has no history of malignancy and no systemic metabolic abnormality.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: A primary bone sarcoma arising within skeletal muscle
Metastatic calcification due to hyperphosphatemia
Metaplasia of connective tissue with bone formation after trauma
Fat necrosis with saponification of peripancreatic fat
Dysplasia of muscle fibers with nuclear pleomorphism

explanation_correct: Metaplasia is not limited to epithelia: connective tissue can also undergo metaplasia, and myositis ossificans is the classic example, with formation of bone within muscle after trauma. Reprogrammed mesenchymal cells in the organizing hematoma lay down osteoid that matures into bone, producing a circumscribed ossified mass that is benign and typically self-limited. This is an adaptive change of the stromal compartment, not a neoplasm, and it is unconnected to any disturbance of calcium or phosphate balance.

explanation_incorrect.B: A primary sarcoma would show atypical, infiltrative neoplastic cells and malignant matrix, not a circumscribed rim of mature lamellar bone following a recognized injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metastatic calcification deposits calcium in normal tissues because of hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia, usually in kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa; this patient has a localized post-traumatic lesion with normal chemistries.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fat necrosis from pancreatic lipase activity occurs in acute pancreatitis or after breast trauma and shows chalky-white saponified fat, not organized bone within muscle.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dysplasia is a disordered, precancerous epithelial process with pleomorphism and loss of orientation; it is not a description of ossification within skeletal muscle.

educationalObjective: Myositis ossificans, bone formation within muscle after trauma, illustrates metaplasia of connective tissue.
